name: 12-week study plan
intro: A BABOK v3 study group usually works the chapters in a fixed order over twelve weeks, one or two knowledge areas a session, with the related techniques alongside. This sequences what is already here to that order, so each week you can drill exactly the ground that week covered. The plan is only a running order: nothing here is drawn from any particular group's materials.
closing: Weeks 3 to 11 are the six knowledge areas and carry the blueprint weighting. Weeks 1, 2 and 12 are Key Concepts and Perspectives — outside the blueprint percentages, examinable all the same, and the ground candidates most often leave until last.

weeks.title: Introduction and the core concept model
weeks.focus: The six core concepts and how they constrain each other. Get this right and the rest of the guide reads as one argument rather than six.
weeks.watch: Change, need, solution, stakeholder, value and context are equal. Any question that lets you settle one without checking the others is testing whether you know that.

weeks.title: Key concepts and requirements classification
weeks.focus: Requirement against design, and the four classes: business, stakeholder, solution, transition.
weeks.watch: Requirement and design are separated by intent, never by level of detail or by project phase. Transition requirements lapse once the transition is done.

weeks.title: Strategy Analysis, part 1
weeks.focus: Analyse the current state and define the future state.
weeks.watch: Current state work is diagnosis, not design. An item that jumps from a recurring failure to a solution is testing whether you stopped to find the cause.

weeks.title: Strategy Analysis, part 2
weeks.focus: Assess risks and define the change strategy.
weeks.watch: Mitigation changes a risk, it does not close it. And a positive return is not the same as the best option — the exam repeatedly offers one that is profitable and beaten.

weeks.title: Solution Evaluation
weeks.focus: Measure performance, analyse measures, assess limitations inside and outside the solution, and recommend action.
weeks.watch: Whether the limitation sits in the solution or in the enterprise around it decides the task, and the two are the most commonly confused pair in this area.

weeks.title: Elicitation and Collaboration
weeks.focus: Prepare, conduct, confirm, communicate, and manage collaboration.
weeks.watch: Choosing the instrument is most of it: interviews go deep with few, surveys go wide with many, observation catches what people cannot articulate, workshops produce an agreed output.

weeks.title: Requirements Analysis and Design Definition, part 1
weeks.watch: Verification asks whether the requirement is well written; validation asks whether it delivers value. Both use reviews, so read what the reviewers are being asked to judge.

weeks.title: Requirements Analysis and Design Definition, part 2
weeks.focus: Requirements architecture, design options, and the value-based recommendation.
weeks.watch: Analysing potential value is business analysis; producing a delivery schedule for the options is project management. The distinction is examined repeatedly.

weeks.title: Requirements Life Cycle Management
weeks.focus: Trace, maintain, prioritise, assess changes, approve.
weeks.watch: Prioritisation has several bases and value is only one. A regulatory date or a dependency governs before value does.

weeks.title: Business Analysis Planning and Monitoring, part 1
weeks.focus: Plan the approach and plan stakeholder engagement.
weeks.watch: Identifying and positioning stakeholders is analysis; deciding how often and how formally to deal with each is engagement planning. Producing a map is not having a plan.

weeks.title: Business Analysis Planning and Monitoring, part 2
weeks.focus: Governance, information management, and improving business analysis performance.
weeks.watch: Governance is who decides and how change is controlled; information management is how the analysis itself is stored, traced and reused. They are easy to blur.

weeks.title: Perspectives
weeks.focus: Agile, business intelligence, information technology, business architecture and business process management.
weeks.watch: Perspectives are not exclusive and none is a house style. More than one commonly applies to the same change, and the approach follows the work rather than the team's habit.
